overview.title: 📖 Overview: Mapping Every Position Around the Stove
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 37a–37b
overview.hebrewSource: מִצְטַמֵּק וְיָפֶה לוֹ — אָסוּר, מִצְטַמֵּק וְרַע לוֹ — מוּתָּר
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The Gemara works through the unresolved question from the previous daf — does the mishna's 'he may not place' mean 'return' or 'leave'? — by reconstructing the mishna's missing text and testing it against parallel Tosefta traditions attributed to Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda. It then maps out every physical position relative to a stove (inside, on top, leaning against), addresses a stove whose ashes reignite on Shabbat, and closes with a detailed dispute over which cooked foods may safely be left on the fire — resolved by Rav Nachman's rule about shriveling and flour.

slides.title: 🧩 Reconstructing the Mishna's Missing Clause
slides.subtitle: The Gemara concludes the mishna is about returning — but only after filling a gap

nodes.content: ❓ If the mishna means 'return,' why does its first clause never mention leaving a pot at all?
💡 The mishna is 'chaseirah mechusrah' — incomplete, and a clause about leaving must be inserted before the Beit Shammai/Beit Hillel dispute over hot water vs. cooked food

columns.label: Rabbi Meir's Tosefta
columns.content: On two adjoining stoves, all agree: once removed, a pot may never be returned

columns.label: Rabbi Yehuda's Tosefta
columns.content: Beit Shammai/Beit Hillel dispute both what may be left and what may be returned

nodes.content: ✅ Our mishna matches Rabbi Yehuda on hot water/cooked food and remove/return — but disagrees with him on one point: our mishna permits leaving food even on an unswept stove

slides.title: 🪢 Four Positions Around an Unswept, Uncovered Stove
slides.subtitle: Inside, on top, leaning against, and returning to it — each has its own rule
rows: Rav in the name of Rabbi Chelbo — coals inside risk being stoked
Place on top (to leave from before Shabbat)
Permitted, per our mishna's first reading
Food already cooking needs no further heat
Tosefta: one may lean against a pomace/wood stove; only placing inside requires sweeping or ash
Beit Hillel permits only on a properly swept/ashed stove

callout.label: Ash-like coals:
callout.text: Coals that have dimmed, or that are covered with a strip of fine flax, count as though the stove were properly ashed — no additional ash is required.

slides.title: 🔥♻️ When a Covered Stove Reignites on Shabbat
slides.subtitle: Rav Oshaya's ruling, extended by Rabbi Yochanan
slides.hebrewSource: קְטָמָהּ וְהוּבְעֲרָה מְשַׁהִין עָלֶיהָ חַמִּין שֶׁהוּחַמּוּ כׇּל צוֹרְכָּן
slides.label: The ruling:
slides.text: If a stove was properly covered with ash before Shabbat and then reignites on its own during Shabbat, Rav Oshaya rules one may still leave on it hot water that was already fully heated and food already fully cooked — since nothing more is needed from the fire, there is no worry that anyone will stoke the coals. Rabbi Yochanan extends this even to unusually hot broom-wood coals, and Rav Safra transmits in Rav Chiyya's name that one may even lean against, leave on, remove from, and return to such a reignited stove — though the Gemara stresses this leniency flows specifically from the ash-covering done before Shabbat, not from any general rule about fully-cooked food.

slides.title: 🥘 May Fully-Cooked Food That Still Improves Be Left on the Fire?
slides.subtitle: A dispute over 'mitztamek v'yafeh lo' — food that shrivels and gets better

lines.speaker: R. Shmuel b.Y.
lines.text: In Rabbi Yochanan's name: one may leave fully-cooked food and fully-heated water on a pomace/wood stove — even food that shrivels and improves the longer it sits.

lines.speaker: A colleague
lines.text: But didn't Rav and Shmuel both rule that food which shrivels-and-improves is forbidden to leave on the fire, precisely because one might be tempted to stoke the coals?

lines.speaker: R. Shmuel b.Y.
lines.text: I know that ruling well — but what I told you follows Rabbi Yochanan's opinion, not Rav and Shmuel's.

lines.speaker: Rav Ukva
lines.text: To Rav Ashi: you who live near where Rav and Shmuel taught should follow them; we will follow Rabbi Yochanan.

callout.label: An unresolved memory:
callout.text: Rav Ashi recalled that fried fish (kasa deharsena) was once left for Rav Huna on Shabbat, but wasn't sure if that was because shrivel-and-improve is permitted, or simply because that floury dish actually shrivels-and-deteriorates.

slides.title: 🌰 Rav Nachman's Rule: What Shrivels and Improves?
slides.subtitle: A practical guide to which dishes may be left on the fire

steps.content: 1️⃣ General principle: mitztamek v'yafeh lo (shrivels and improves) is forbidden to leave; mitztamek v'ra lo (shrivels and deteriorates) is permitted
2️⃣ Any dish containing flour shrivels-and-deteriorates — with one exception: turnip stew, which improves even though it has flour
3️⃣ This 'improves' rule for turnip stew applies only when meat is in it; without meat, it deteriorates like other floury dishes
4️⃣ Even with meat, it only improves when not intended for guests — food meant for guests is considered to deteriorate, since overcooked food is unappetizing to serve
5️⃣ Figs, porridge, and dates all shrivel and deteriorate when left on the fire, and so may be left

summary.principle: Whether food may be left, leaned, or returned to a stove on Shabbat depends on precise physical position (inside, on top, or against it), on whether the stove was swept or ashed, and — for fully-cooked food — on whether it actually improves or deteriorates the longer it sits on the fire.

flowSteps.content: 🧩 The mishna's missing clause is restored, matching it to Rabbi Yehuda's Tosefta on one point, disagreeing on another
🪢 Placing inside is always forbidden unswept; leaning against is always permitted; returning needs sweeping or ash
🔥 A properly ash-covered stove that reignites still allows leaving fully-cooked, fully-heated food — even from broom-wood coals

columns.content: 🥘 Rabbi Yochanan permits leaving shrivel-and-improve food; Rav and Shmuel forbid it
🌰 Rav Nachman: flour dishes deteriorate except turnip stew with meat, not for guests

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: food that needs no further improvement from the fire may be left; food that would benefit from more heat may not, lest one stoke the coals

quiz.q: What does the Gemara mean when it says the mishna is 'chaseirah mechusrah' (incomplete)?
o: The mishna has a scribal error that cannot be fixed
A clause about leaving a pot on the stove must be inserted for the mishna to make full sense
The mishna is missing an entire chapter
Beit Shammai's opinion was accidentally omitted
quiz.e: The Gemara resolves the mishna by supplying a missing clause about leaving a pot on the stove, which then sets up the later Beit Shammai/Beit Hillel dispute properly.

quiz.q: According to the Tosefta, is it permitted to lean a pot against an unswept, uncovered stove heated with pomace or wood?
o: No, leaning is treated the same as placing inside
Yes — only placing food inside the stove requires it to be swept or ashed
It is permitted only on Friday, never on Shabbat
It is permitted only for hot water, never for cooked food
quiz.e: The Tosefta distinguishes leaning (permitted even unswept) from placing inside (forbidden unswept).

quiz.q: What does Rav Oshaya permit leaving on a stove that was properly covered with ash before Shabbat but then reignites?
o: Nothing at all, until it is re-covered
Any food, regardless of how cooked it is
Hot water and food that are already fully heated/cooked
Only cold food that has not yet been touched by fire
quiz.e: Rav Oshaya rules that fully-heated water and fully-cooked food may be left, since there is no concern one will stoke the coals for food that needs nothing more.

quiz.q: Why does Rav and Shmuel's ruling on 'mitztamek v'yafeh lo' (shrivels and improves) forbid leaving such food on the fire, according to the dispute on this daf?
o: Because it violates the laws of tithing
Because there is concern one will stoke the coals to further improve it
Because it is not kosher once shriveled
Because it must be eaten within an hour of cooking
quiz.e: Food that would benefit from continued heat creates a temptation to stoke the coals, which is why Rav and Shmuel forbid leaving it, though Rabbi Yochanan is more lenient.

quiz.q: According to Rav Nachman's rule, which dish shrivels and improves despite containing flour?
o: Porridge
Dates cooked in syrup
Turnip stew, when it contains meat and is not intended for guests
Any dish with fried fish
quiz.e: Rav Nachman singles out turnip stew as the exception to the rule that floury dishes deteriorate — but only when it has meat and is not being prepared for guests.
